heading: 1 Introduction (1.1 Problem Background, 1.2 Restatement, 1.3 Literature Review, 1.4 Our Work)
note: 18 blocks, 417 words. The '1 Introduction' heading rides in the tail of block 25 (last contents line) and the 1.3 heading in 33's tail. 26 is the background with the $26.5 billion figure and the zoonosis claim, both cited to [1] and [2]. 27-33 are the five problem statements, one line each, and they are not the five competition tasks — they are the paper's own restatement (target identification, project development, rights and resources, measures of IWT, likelihood of success), which the body then maps onto Tasks 1-5 in a different order. 34-35 are a two-paragraph literature review: zoonoses and crime links in the first, captive breeding and protected areas as prior interventions in the second, with five references in four sentences. 36 announces the five-step work plan and 37-41 are the five bullets, one paragraph each. 42 announces the workflow and 43 is the Figure 1 caption with the '2 Assumptions' heading glued into its tail — the only caption in the paper that arrives with a chapter heading attached.

heading: 2 Assumptions
note: 4 blocks, 39 words — the shortest assumptions section of the three 2024 IWT papers read so far, and the one with no justifications at all. The three assumptions are: the smallest participant in the global IWT is measured by country; the social environment is relatively stable; and 'The data we collect is precise and representative'. The third is the one that matters, since the whole paper is a data-driven network exercise on CITES trade records and a claimed 193-country, 36-year panel, and it is asserted in seven words with no discussion of reporting bias, seizure rates or CITES coverage. 47's tail carries the '3 Notations' heading.

heading: 3 Notations (Table 1)
note: 4 blocks, 90 words. 48 is the lead and the Table 1 caption; 49-51 are the table body, and the extraction interleaved the symbols with their descriptions — 49 gives β, δ, γ (prey growth, predation, predator mortality), IWT, PUR, SR, PER, IN, CI, SC, SD, GA and a truncated INO, 50 completes INO and PAP, and 51 finishes with SE, OSR, TTV and CAI. Note the symbol clash that the table creates and the body never resolves: β and δ are the Lotka-Volterra predation and energy-conversion rates in Table 1 and simultaneously the coefficients of the regression in section 6.3, and α, used in block 67 for the prey growth rate, is absent from the table. 51's tail carries the '4 Data preprocessing / 4.1 Data collection' headings.

heading: 4 Data preprocessing (4.1 Data collection, 4.2 Data normalization)
note: 14 blocks, 309 words. 52-53 describe the collection and its purpose, and 54 gives the only quantitative scope in the chapter: '193 countries for 36 years (1986-2021)' from cites [8]. That is 6,948 country-years, and the 36-year panel is never used at that resolution anywhere in the paper — the client scores are single numbers, the Lotka-Volterra fit uses 'the data of all the years' without stating which, and the BP network trains on 248 records. 55-58 are equations (1)-(4), a min-max style standardisation written with badly garbled subscripts ('x_i = (x_i − x_best)/M' followed by a piecewise re-definition at a and b), 59-61 equations (5)-(7) define the matrix X, its normalisation Z and the transposed product, and 62-65 close with the specific-gravity matrix P and equation (8)-(9), ending on 'We think of ratio (8) as a probability' with the chapter 5 heading in the tail. The normalisation block is the paper's only mathematical preamble and it is never referenced again: PUR, SR and PER are normalised 'to obtain the results shown in Figure 3' with no equation tying them to (5)-(9).

heading: 5 Lotka-Volterra integrated evaluation model for task1 (5.1 Modeling population competition, 5.2 Model solution)
note: 17 blocks, 495 words. The conceit is stated flatly in 66: international conservation organisations are the predator and poachers the prey, so 'the vitality ... presents a population competition relationship with the stealers'. 67-71 define the four parameters as prose (prey growth rate 'estimated by the natural growth trend of illegal trade activities'; predation rate as encounters times enforcement efficiency; predator mortality as 1/funding level; energy conversion as people's support times political support), and 72 prints equation (10) with the α, β, γ, δ symbols. 73 then collapses the model to three quantities — PUR = β, SR = δ, PER = 1/γ — so the AHP that follows scores three proxies rather than the four parameters, and α, the one parameter that describes the poachers' own growth, disappears from the evaluation entirely. 76 scores PUR, SR and PER; 77 is the pairwise matrix (11) (1, 2, 1.25 / 0.5, 1, 0.625 / 0.8, 1.6, 1), which is exactly consistent, and 78 reports the weights as PUR 0.43, PER 0.35, SR 0.22 — reproducible as the normalised row sums (4.25 / 9.775 = 0.435, 3.4 / 9.775 = 0.348, 2.125 / 9.775 = 0.217). 79-81 repeat the exercise for the benefit side with matrix (12) and weights 0.44 / 0.33 / 0.23, again reproducible by row sums (4.33 / 9.75 = 0.444, 3.25 / 9.75 = 0.333, 2.17 / 9.75 = 0.222). Both matrices are exactly consistent, so their CR would be zero, and the paper reports neither CR nor the eigenvector — it reports row-sum weights, which coincide with the principal eigenvector only because the matrices are consistent. 82 is the Figure 2 caption, covering both weight charts.

heading: 5.3 Analysis and comparison (client selection)
note: 12 blocks, 357 words. 83 names the three candidate clients (GA, INO, PAP) and 84-86 characterise each in one bullet, with the fitness logic already visible: GA has funding and political support but wants reputation, INO has global reach and wants species diversity, PAP is effective locally but wants tangible benefits. 87 scores them on the five elements and 88 is the caption for Figure 3. 89-90 read the radar chart (PER strongest for GA at 0.81, CI and IN strongest for INO at 0.70 and 0.443, SR and PUR strongest for PAP at 0.86 and 0.71), and 90 ends by repeating its own last sentence almost verbatim — 'Both PUR and SR are most attractive to PAP, both are relatively weak to INO, and both are least attractive to GA' appears twice in the same printed paragraph. 91 gives the composite, CAI = (1 + IN)(CI · SC) + (1 + IN · CI)(0.43 PUR + 0.22 SR + 0.35 PER) — note that SC, the 'self condition', appears in the formula and is never assigned a value anywhere in the paper, so the composite cannot be reproduced. 92-93 print Table 2 with the five indicator values and the three scores (0.42, 0.51, 0.37) and 94 selects INO. Worth recording that the winner is also the client whose weakest dimension, per 89, is IN at 0.43 and CI at 0.70 — the highest of the three on both — so the ranking is driven by the fifth element the text never discusses.

heading: 6 BP neural network prediction model for task2 (6.1 Reduce the number of poaching organization, 6.2 Improve biodiversity)
note: 14 blocks, 399 words, and the section where the figure numbering breaks. 96 says the poaching-organisation data cover 2000-2020 and the linear fit is 'shown in Figure 5 below'; 99 then prints the captions as 'Figure 4: Linear fit of the natural growth' and 'Figure 5: Dynamics', so the text has already pointed at the wrong number before the figure appears. 97 refits the Lotka-Volterra system to the data and prints equation (14) with numbers (dX/dt = 0.038X − 0.37452XY, and a second line the extraction renders as '−0.30277XY 0.322203 0.1Y', i.e. the interaction and mortality terms are fused and the sign of the predation term is unreadable as printed), with X(0) = 0.19 and Y(0) = 0.2. 100-102 read the two panels: poaching organisations trending up on their own, then falling once the model is applied, with 'a substantial decrease in the degree of hierarchy'. 103-104 turn to biodiversity through the Pathare study and Project Tiger, and 105-106 write the link as SD = C · (Decline in poaching groups) (15) — a proportionality with an unnamed constant C and no data. 107 then cites 'Figure 6' for the poaching effect, but Figure 6 is the BP network flowchart (caption at 117); and 108 converts the whole thing into the paper's biodiversity claim, 'the level of conservation of species diversity will increase by about 21% in five years', which has no derivation — C is undefined and equation (15) has no units. 108's tail carries the '6.3 / 6.3.1' headings.

heading: 6.3.1 BP Neural Network (equations)
note: 9 blocks, 168 words. This is a textbook derivation with no application: 109-110 give neuron output y_j = σ(Σ ω_ij x_i + b_j) (16) and define the symbols, 111-112 the mean-square loss (17), 113 the weight and bias update rules (18)-(19), 114 the chain rule (20), and 115 the stopping rule. Every symbol is generic — ω_ij, b_j, d_p, y_p, η — and none of them is connected to PUR, SR, PER, the five trade categories or the poaching counts. The paper reports that a network was trained (block 119) but never states its architecture: no layer count, no neuron count, no learning rate, no activation function, and no statement of what the input vector is. 116 announces the flowchart and 117 is its caption.

heading: 6.3.2 Training of BP Neural Network
note: 4 blocks, 86 words, and the only report of model performance in the paper. 119 gives the training run: 248 data, 736 iterations, about 29 seconds. 121 reads Figure 7 as R = 0.997 for training, 0.939 for validation, 0.929 for test and 'the R of training is 0.923' — the fourth label is a duplicate of the first, so one of the four values has no name and the correlation of the full set is unstated. The abstract's 'R-value of the model training result is about 0.966' matches none of the four printed numbers. No MSE, no target threshold, no statement of how the 248 records were split, and no baseline — a network fitted to 248 points with 736 iterations and an R of 0.997 on its own training set says nothing about forecasting skill, which is what the next section uses it for.

heading: 6.3.3 Forecast future volumes
note: 5 blocks, 132 words. 122 predicts the next five years of global IWT with the trained network and 123 is the Figure 8 caption. 124 makes the validation argument, and it is a self-comparison: 'the height of our predicted data for the next 5 years is about the same as that of the historical data with similar fluctuations, which is consistent with the historical trend in terms of the pattern, and it can be shown that our predicted data are reasonable.' A forecast that reproduces the level and variance of the history is being offered as evidence that the forecast is right, which is the one thing a five-year-ahead extrapolation cannot demonstrate. 125 then states the substantive finding — without intervention the trade stays high — and 126 draws the project's necessity from it. No number appears: the forecast exists only as a curve, so the 'still high' reading has no magnitude and cannot be compared with the 23.5% reduction claimed later.

heading: 7 Project assumptions and network prototyping for task3 (7.1, 7.2, 7.3 strategy constraints)
note: 18 blocks, 506 words. 127 announces the global IWT network with the Figure 9 caption fused into the same block, and 128-129 define the graph (countries as nodes V = {v_i}, directed edges where trade exists, darker nodes for more partners) — a definition split by the page column that only makes sense read together. 130 names the three strategies. Each strategy then follows the same structure: a mechanism paragraph saying which parameter it raises (publicity raises SR, hot-spot strikes raise PUR, fixed-point monitoring raises PER), a claim that INO is the right actor, and a bulleted list of 'powers and conditions'. Those bullets are the model's actual constraints and they are all stated as numbers with no source: propagandists stay 7 days per country and travel no more than 8 hours at a time at 120 km/h; one node takes a year to destroy and stays down five years; a monitoring point takes a year to establish and its area is fixed but unspecified. The 8-hour and 120 km/h pair is the one that later produces the 1,696-day tour, and nothing justifies either: 8 hours at 120 km/h is 960 km per hop, which is a car journey applied to a worldwide itinerary.

heading: 8 Analysis of Big Data Transaction Networks for task4 (8.1 TSP and simulated annealing, 8.2 node strikes, 8.3 monitoring, 8.4 effectiveness)
note: 41 blocks, 1022 words — the longest chapter by far, and it runs four separate models. 147-154 are the TSP formulation (equations 21-24: distance matrix, binary decision variable, minimise total distance, one entry and one exit per city), all standard and all unused in the outcome: the tour is never solved with these constraints, it is solved by simulated annealing. 155-162 give the annealing machinery (objective, cooling schedule T_new = αT_current, Metropolis acceptance, neighbourhood perturbation) with no parameter values — α, T_0, the stopping criterion and the number of restarts are all missing. 164 is the result: 166 countries, 'about 1,696 days' for the global tour. Check the arithmetic: 166 countries at 7 days each is 1,162 days, leaving 534 days of travel, or 12,816 hours at 120 km/h, about 64,000 km per hop — a figure that no route list supports and that the appendix table (block 266, a bare list of 166 country codes) cannot corroborate. 165-170 then attach the persuasion model: the survey table gives 87.0% strongly agreeing, and equation (29) states the growth rate of support as 0.9568 × promotional progress, a coefficient with no derivation. 172-175 handle the strike strategy with equation (30), SE = 1/Node size and OSR = SE × TTV, and report that trade falls rapidly in 2024-2028 and gently in 2028-2029 — 2029 is outside the five-year window. 176-182 choose the monitoring countries by a greedy rule and print coordinates and a 1000 km radius; the ordering sentence in 178 ('countries with large IWT establishing surveillance systems first') is contradicted by the order it then lists, which begins with Switzerland. 183-185 report the combined effect as a 23.5% reduction read off a heat map, with the caption numbering broken again: 183 points at 'Figure 16' and 184 prints 'Figure 13: The before and after comparison of IWT'.

heading: 9 Probabilistic model of project implementation for task5 / 9.1 Forecasting the likelihood of meeting expectations
note: 14 blocks, 304 words. 187 sets the success criterion — all three strategies at 95% within five years. 188-191 enumerate the three impediments (flight delays, poaching-organisation resistance, bad weather) in three bullets. 192 gives the two binomial probabilities, 15.36% for delays and 10% for resistance, 'based on the data of the past years', and 193 gives the weather as Poisson with λ = 30 — no unit for the 30, no source for any of the three. 194-196 assemble the three attainment functions and solve equations (33)-(34) for the capacity bounds K1 ≤ 28, K2 ≤ 1.25, K3 ≤ 45.625; the printed constraints are three lines long and do not obviously produce those numbers (K2 = 1.25 people is not a capacity, it is a fractional person). 198 restates the method as an 'n-weight Bernoulli test'. 199 is the answer: P = 0.8286 · 0.9185 · 0.9960 = 65.1%, and the three factors are the probabilities that each constraint is met. The multiplication is valid only under independence, which is asserted nowhere, and the 65.1% is the paper's headline project probability — quoted in the abstract, the sensitivity section and the memo.

heading: 9.2 Contextual sensitivity analysis
note: 6 blocks, 273 words, three one-at-a-time perturbations of 10%. Flight delay impact +10% moves K to 25 and the first factor from 0.8286 to 0.8075, 'a decrease of about 2.5%' — the arithmetic gives 2.55%, so the label matches. Poaching resistance +10% drops the second factor from 0.9185 to 0.7373, 'a decrease of about 19.73%' — again consistent. Bad weather days +10% moves the Poisson factor from 0.996 to 0.9275, 'about 6.8%' — 0.996 to 0.9275 is a 6.88% relative drop, consistent. What the section never does is recompute the total: 204 and 205 state that resistance is the binding factor and that under it 'the total project to meet the expectations rate will be reduced to 60.8%', but 0.8286 · 0.7373 · 0.9960 = 60.9%, so the number is the product of the other two unchanged factors and is correct only if the three are independent — the same assumption this section's whole design rests on, still unstated. No perturbation of λ or of the 95% goal, and no interval or distribution: 'sensitivity' here means three point shifts.

heading: 10 Model Evaluation (10.1 Strengths, 10.2 Weaknesses)
note: 6 blocks, 186 words. The four strengths are a single bullet each: big-data drive with probability theory and neural networks; a global IWT network visualised; three optimization models producing specific solutions; and unexpected factors included. Three of the four are restatements of what the paper did rather than findings about the model. The two weaknesses are more informative. 210 concedes the stability assumption and says the attainment rate absorbs social shocks, which is a claim rather than a diagnosis. 211 is the paper's one honest limit: 'We have not yet computed the data for all countries in the world' — and this is the crucial admission, because block 54 claims 193 countries and 36 years while block 164 solves the tour on 166, block 177 picks monitoring countries from a subset, and the whole network is built on whatever fraction was actually processed. 211's tail carries the 'Memo' heading.

heading: Memo — To: INO, Subject: Cooperation On Reducing The Illegal Wildlife Trade
note: 32 blocks, 468 words. 212 is the header block (Date: February 5, 2024; To: INO; From: Team # 2417340; Subject). 213-214 introduce the memo and announce 'a table below describing the details', and that table is the rest of the memo: fifteen year-by-year rows in three strategy columns, which the extraction splits so that the year text, the strategy name column and the third column are interleaved one fragment per block — hence the fifteen read-figure groups, five per strategy. The table is where all the memo's numbers live: 33 countries visited in year one, global support +19.02% in year two rising to 95.68% by year five, IWT −4.8% in year two of the strike strategy, a first monitoring station in the capital of 'SC' with 50 technicians, then East Asia, the United States and South Africa. Three inconsistencies are worth recording: the first-year route 'starts with LBN' although the appendix route list (block 266) begins with LI and BG; 'start the publicity from SE' uses an abbreviation that is never defined, in a memo whose audience is told nothing about the appendix codes; and the memo's 19.02% and 95.68% support figures appear in no body section — the body's support model (equation 29) has no such numbers. 242 and 243 close with the request for adoption, and 243's tail carries 'References'.
